name: Sendai and Matsushima
tagline: Gyutan and zunda, plus the sea of 260 islands, all in one trip
intro: Use quiet Sendai, with its tree-lined zelkova avenues, as your base. From here, Matsushima, one of Japan's Three Views, is a 40-minute train ride for an island cruise, Akiu Onsen is 50 minutes by bus, and Yamadera, the temple of a thousand steps, is about an hour by train. It is a food destination built around gyutan (beef tongue), zunda (edamame) sweets, oysters and fresh fish, and it is never overcrowded, so two women traveling together and families with children can both take it at an easy pace. Add photogenic stops like Zao Fox Village and Ginzan Onsen and 3 nights is the right length.
season_notes: Spring (mid-April to May): cherry blossoms peak in mid-April, and Saigyo Modoshi no Matsu Park lets you frame the blossoms and Matsushima Bay in a single shot. Summer (July to August): the Tanabata Festival on August 6 to 8 fills the shopping arcades with decorations, and the rainy season lasts until mid-July. Autumn (October to November): the foliage at Akiu Great Falls and Yamadera peaks from late October to early November, and oyster season begins. Winter (December to February): the Pageant of Starlight on Jozenji-dori in December, and snowy Fox Village and Ginzan Onsen are the highlights, but snow boots are a must.
airport_access/0/note: 17 minutes by rapid, 25 minutes by local. Trains run every 20 to 30 minutes. Fares are as of 2026 (to be confirmed)
airport_access/1/mode: JR Sendai Airport Access Line + Senseki Line
airport_access/1/note: Transfer to the Senseki Line at Sendai Station. The fare is a rough total of both legs (to be confirmed)
airport_access/2/note: There is a route that goes straight to the hot spring inns, but departures are few. Whether it is running and the fare are to be confirmed
getting_around: Use the Loople Sendai sightseeing loop bus, which leaves from the bus pool west of Sendai Station, to circle the city sights (Sendai Castle Ruins, Zuihoden, Osaki Hachimangu). Matsushima is on the JR Senseki Line, Yamadera on the JR Senzan Line, and Akiu on the Miyagi Kotsu bus, all departing from Sendai Station, so the key is to group one direction per day. The gyutan street around the station, the shopping arcades and Jozenji-dori are all within walking distance.
transport_pass: Loople Sendai 1-day ticket: ¥630 (includes discounts on admission to city sights). Sendai Marugoto Pass 2-day ticket: ¥2,720 (unlimited JR and bus rides to Matsushima, Yamadera, Akiu and the Sendai Airport Line). Prices are as of 2026 (to be confirmed)
spots/0/desc: The gateway to Tohoku is small, so arrival and departure go quickly. Souvenir shops cluster on the 2nd-floor departure level, which makes it a good place for last-minute Hagi no Tsuki, zunda sweets and canned gyutan.
spots/0/access: JR Sendai Airport Station, connected directly to the 1st-floor arrivals lobby
spots/0/hours: Shops are generally open 7:30 to 20:00 (to be confirmed)
spots/0/tip: International departures are few, so check-in counters open late. Arriving 2 hours before departure is enough.
spots/0/kid_tip: The 3rd-floor observation deck gives a close view of takeoffs and landings.
spots/1/desc: This is the hub of your trip, where the Shinkansen, Senseki Line, Senzan Line and Airport Line all meet. The 3rd-floor Gyutan Street and Zunda Alley, plus Espal and S-PAL underground, bring all the local specialties together, so you can spend a rainy day entirely inside the station.
spots/1/access: 17 to 25 minutes from the airport by JR
spots/1/tip: Loople Sendai leaves from Stop 16 at the west exit bus pool. Coin lockers in the station are plentiful for luggage.
spots/1/kid_tip: Lunch lines at Gyutan Street on the 3rd floor are long, so we recommend getting in before 11:00.
spots/2/desc: The symbol of Sendai is a 700 m avenue lined with zelkova trees. Sculptures stand along the central promenade, and in December the Pageant of Starlight lights up the whole avenue with bulbs.
spots/2/access: 1 minute on foot from Kotodai-koen Station on the Namboku subway line
spots/2/tip: The prettiest times are the September jazz festival, the October foliage and the December Pageant of Starlight.
spots/2/kid_tip: At the end of the avenue, Kotodai Park has a fountain and lawns, so it is a nice place to rest.
spots/3/desc: This glass building designed by architect Toyo Ito houses a library and galleries. The ground-floor cafe and shop are pleasant, and from the 6th floor you can see the avenue trees of Jozenji-dori.
spots/3/access: 6 minutes on foot from Kotodai-koen Station
spots/3/closed: Fourth Thursday of every month (to be confirmed)
spots/3/tip: A good place to rest on a rainy day or a hot afternoon during your walk along the avenue.
spots/3/kid_tip: There is a children's book corner on the 1st floor.
spots/4/desc: This covered shopping street runs from Sendai Station to Jozenji-dori, with shops selling gyutan, zunda and kamaboko, plus drugstores. During the Tanabata Festival in August, huge decorations fill the arcade.
spots/4/access: 5 minutes on foot from the west exit of Sendai Station
spots/4/tip: You can walk from the station to Jozenji-dori without an umbrella, even on rainy days.
spots/4/kid_tip: There are many gacha and character shops in the arcade, which kids love.
spots/5/desc: This local market in the alley west of the station has more than 70 fish, vegetable and side dish shops. The seafood rice bowl shops and tempura stalls are good for a light breakfast or early lunch.
spots/5/access: 5 minutes on foot from the west exit of Sendai Station
spots/5/tip: In strawberry season (January to April), you can buy packs of Miyagi strawberries cheaply.
spots/5/kid_tip: Try the kamaboko skewers sold in front of the shops as a snack.
spots/6/desc: This is the mausoleum of Date Masamune, lord of the Sendai domain. At the top of a staircase through a cedar forest, a gorgeous Momoyama-style building appears. It is quiet and shady, so it is pleasant to walk even in summer.
spots/6/access: Get off at Loople Sendai's Zuihoden-mae stop and walk 7 minutes (uphill)
spots/6/tip: Show your Loople 1-day ticket for an admission discount. There are many stairs, so sneakers are a must.
spots/6/kid_tip: Strollers are difficult because of the stairs. We recommend a baby carrier.
spots/7/desc: There is no castle keep, but the main draw is the equestrian statue of Date Masamune and the view over Sendai. Next door, the Aoba Castle Exhibition Hall shows the castle restored in CG.
spots/7/access: Get off at Loople Sendai's Sendai-jo-ato stop, right at the site
spots/7/hours: Ruins always open; exhibition hall 9:00 to 17:00 (until 16:00 from November to March, to be confirmed)
spots/7/tip: The night view at dusk is lovely, but the last Loople bus (around 16:00) will have left, so take a taxi or city bus back.
spots/7/kid_tip: The plaza in front of the statue is wide and good for running around, and there is a zunda shake stand.
spots/8/desc: It displays relics of the Date clan, including Date Masamune's crescent-moon helmet and armor. It is just below the castle ruins, so it is easy to combine the two.
spots/8/access: Get off at Loople Sendai's Hakubutsukan-Kokusai Center-mae stop and walk 3 minutes
spots/8/closed: Mondays, and the day after a national holiday
spots/8/tip: Since the renewal, the exhibit explanations are easier to follow, and there are Korean signs.
spots/8/kid_tip: There is an armor experience corner that kids love.
spots/9/desc: This National Treasure shrine was built by Date Masamune. The main hall, in black lacquer with gold decoration, is gorgeous. The cedar forest along the approach is deep and calm even though you are in the city.
spots/9/access: Get off at Loople Sendai's Osaki-Hachimangu-mae stop and walk 3 minutes
spots/9/tip: It is one of the last stops on the Loople route, so going in the morning first leaves you extra time.
spots/9/kid_tip: About 100 steps. Short enough to carry a small child up.
spots/10/desc: This municipal zoo is reachable directly by subway and has elephants, giraffes and polar bears. Admission is cheap and the grounds are hilly, so it makes a half-day outing.
spots/10/access: 3 minutes on foot from Yagiyama-Dobutsukoen Station on the Tozai subway line
spots/10/closed: Wednesdays (the next day if it is a national holiday)
spots/10/tip: From the rooftop observatory at the station you can see over Sendai.
spots/10/kid_tip: Check the big-cat feeding times at the entrance. You may bring your own lunch.
spots/11/desc: This indoor theme facility is a walk from the east exit of Sendai Station and is the most popular choice for families with preschoolers. The museum charges admission, while the shopping mall is free.
spots/11/access: 9 minutes on foot from the east exit of Sendai Station
spots/11/tip: The admission fee is the same for ages 1 and up. It is a good rainy-day alternative.
spots/11/kid_tip: The Anpanman bakery in the mall can be used without an admission ticket.
spots/12/desc: This modern aquarium has a large tank recreating the Sanriku sea, plus dolphin and sea lion shows. Right next to the Mitsui Outlet, the two make a good half-day course.
spots/12/access: 15 minutes on foot from Nakanosakae Station on the JR Senseki Line, or take the free shuttle
spots/12/hours: 9:00 to 17:30 (varies by season, to be confirmed)
spots/12/tip: Entering in time for the dolphin show makes your route easier. Fares are as of 2026 (to be confirmed).
spots/12/kid_tip: The penguin and otter feeding experiences are first come, first served on the day.
spots/13/desc: This open-air outlet with a Ferris wheel has many sports, outdoor and general goods brands. It is a 5-minute walk from the aquarium, so it makes a half-day for a family trip.
spots/13/access: 8 minutes on foot from Nakanosakae Station on the JR Senseki Line
spots/13/tip: There is a tax-free counter. The Ferris wheel costs extra.
spots/13/kid_tip: The food court and Ferris wheel make it easy to give kids a rest.
spots/14/desc: This 50-minute cruise around Matsushima Bay, dotted with some 260 islands, is the easiest way to feel why it is one of Japan's Three Views. You pass rock formations like Niojima and Sengan-jima with an announcer's commentary.
spots/14/access: 5 minutes on foot from Matsushima-Kaigan Station on the JR Senseki Line, central pier
spots/14/hours: Departs on the hour from 9:00 to 16:00 (to be confirmed)
spots/14/tip: The 2nd-floor Green Class seats cost extra. Feeding the gulls is prohibited. Fares are as of 2026 (to be confirmed).
spots/14/kid_tip: There are indoor seats, so it is fine on windy days.
spots/15/desc: This National Treasure temple was rebuilt by Date Masamune. The cedar-lined approach and the main hall with its gold-leaf wall paintings are the highlights. The cave ruins near the entrance remained intact even after the tsunami.
spots/15/access: 7 minutes on foot from Matsushima-Kaigan Station
spots/15/hours: 8:30 to 17:00 (closes between 15:30 and 16:30 depending on the season, to be confirmed)
spots/15/tip: Treasure hall admission is included. You take your shoes off in the main hall, so bring socks.
spots/15/kid_tip: The path is flat, so strollers work (except inside the main hall).
spots/16/desc: This small temple next to Zuiganji has a moss garden and a rose garden, and is famous for its autumn foliage light-up. The prayer bead making experience is popular with women travelers.
spots/16/access: 6 minutes on foot from Matsushima-Kaigan Station
spots/16/hours: 9:00 to 16:00 (varies by season, to be confirmed)
spots/16/tip: The prayer bead making experience costs around ¥1,000 and takes 30 minutes (to be confirmed).
spots/16/kid_tip: The experience is fine from elementary school age.
spots/17/desc: This symbol of Matsushima stands on a small island in the sea, reached by crossing the red Sukashibashi bridge, where you can see the water through the gaps. It is right next to the shore and the cruise pier, so a visit takes just 5 minutes.
spots/17/access: 6 minutes on foot from Matsushima-Kaigan Station
spots/17/tip: The gaps in the bridge are wide, so avoid heels and hold your child's hand.
spots/17/kid_tip: If your child is afraid of the bridge, carry them across.
spots/18/desc: This natural park island is reached by the 252 m red Fukuura Bridge, and the loop trail takes 30 minutes. The bay view from the lookout inside the island feels different from the cruise.
spots/18/access: 10 minutes on foot from Matsushima-Kaigan Station
spots/18/hours: 8:00 to 17:00 (8:30 to 16:30 from November to February)
spots/18/tip: The bridge toll is ¥200. There are no shops on the island except vending machines.
spots/18/kid_tip: The trail is gentle, so it is good for walking with kids.
spots/19/desc: This lookout park on a hill frames the cherry blossoms and Matsushima Bay in one shot. Rest with a sea view at the cafe Le Roman inside the park.
spots/19/access: 20 minutes on foot from Matsushima-Kaigan Station (uphill) or 5 minutes by taxi
spots/19/tip: Cherry blossoms bloom in mid-April. The uphill path is steep, so leave your bags in a station locker.
spots/19/kid_tip: The path is hard for strollers. We recommend a taxi for kids.
spots/20/desc: Standing atop 202 stone steps, this is the top shrine in Tohoku, where people pray for safety at sea. Shiogama is a sushi town with a large tuna fishery cooperative trade, so pair a visit with a sushi lunch afterward.
spots/20/access: 15 minutes on foot from Hon-Shiogama Station on the JR Senseki Line
spots/20/tip: You can stop by on the way to Matsushima, or take a cruise from Shiogama Port to Matsushima.
spots/20/kid_tip: Instead of the front stairs, take the gentler eastern approach for an easier climb.
spots/21/desc: With a 55 m drop, this is one of Japan's three great waterfalls. You can view it from the observation deck or walk down the stairs to the base. The foliage is most beautiful in late October.
spots/21/access: About 70 minutes by Miyagi Kotsu bus from the west exit of Sendai Station, get off at Akiu-Otaki (few departures, to be confirmed)
spots/21/tip: The path down to the base is a 20-minute round trip of stairs. Check the bus timetable ahead of time and combine it with Akiu Onsen.
spots/21/kid_tip: Strollers can reach the observation deck, but the path below is difficult.
spots/22/desc: At the entrance to the Akiu Onsen village, this gorge has a 650 m walking trail along the Natori River as it flows between rock formations. It suits a 30-minute walk before or after checking in at a hot spring inn.
spots/22/access: Right at the Akiu Onsen bus stop (Nozokibashi)
spots/22/tip: Look for the heart-shaped pool, Oboshi no Heart.
spots/22/kid_tip: There are railings, but the path is rocky, so hold hands.
spots/23/desc: This hot spring village with a 1,500-year history is 50 minutes from Sendai by bus, and is home to large ryokan like Sakan and Iwanumaya. Many inns accept day-trip bathers, so you can enjoy the hot springs without staying overnight.
spots/23/access: About 50 minutes by Miyagi Kotsu bus from Stop 8 at the west exit of Sendai Station, get off at Akiu-Onsen-Yumoto
spots/23/hours: Day-trip bathing varies by inn (generally 11:00 to 15:00)
spots/23/tip: Day-trip bathing fees are an estimate of ¥1,000 to ¥2,000. Get a map and coupons at the Akiu Sato Center.
spots/23/kid_tip: Next to the Sato Center, Akiu Village has a playground and a farm produce market.
spots/24/desc: Red brick buildings line up in a forest at this distillery, which offers free tours and tastings. It is on the way to Yamadera on the Senzan Line, so it is easy to combine the two.
spots/24/access: From Sakunami Station on the JR Senzan Line, take the free shuttle or walk 25 minutes
spots/24/hours: 9:00 to 15:30 (tours by reservation, to be confirmed)
spots/24/closed: New Year holidays, and irregular closures (to be confirmed)
spots/24/tip: Reserve your tour in advance on the official website. Drivers get a non-alcoholic tasting.
spots/24/kid_tip: Children can join the tour, but tasting is for adults only.
spots/25/desc: Made famous by Basho's haiku, this mountain temple has 1,015 stone steps. Standing at the Godaido lookout on the cliff, the whole mountain village comes into view. It is an easy hike of about an hour and a half round trip.
spots/25/access: About 60 minutes from Sendai Station on the JR Senzan Line, then 10 minutes on foot from Yamadera Station
spots/25/hours: 8:00 to 17:00 (last entry to the mountain around 16:00, to be confirmed)
spots/25/tip: The Senzan Line runs 1 to 2 trains an hour. The entrance fee is as of 2026 (to be confirmed). Try a tamakonnyaku skewer in front of the station.
spots/25/kid_tip: Lower elementary school kids can climb it, but strollers and baby carriers are difficult.
spots/26/desc: Over 100 foxes roam freely in this mountain facility, which is famous for photos of foxes in the winter snow. With a 13-minute Shinkansen ride from Sendai and a 20-minute taxi, you can do it in half a day.
spots/26/access: Taxi about 20 minutes from JR Shiroishi-Zao Station (about ¥4,000 estimate), or a weekends-only bus (to be confirmed)
spots/26/tip: Foxes can bite, so do not crouch down and do not let belongings dangle. Fees and closing days are as of 2026 (to be confirmed).
spots/26/kid_tip: The fox holding experience is paid and by time slot. Carry small children.
spots/27/desc: This hot spring town in Yamagata has Taisho-era wooden ryokan lining both sides of a river, and is famous for its gas-lamp scenery on snowy nights. It is a 6-hour round trip from Sendai, so a day trip is tight and one night is best.
spots/27/access: From Sendai Station, about 2 hours via the Senzan Line and Yamagata Shinkansen to Oishida Station, then 40 minutes by bus (to be confirmed)
spots/27/hours: Town always open; for day-trip bathing, the public bath Shirogane-yu is open around 9:00 to 16:00 (to be confirmed)
spots/27/tip: In peak winter season, entry restrictions and reservations may be enforced in the town, so checking the official notice before your visit is a must.
spots/27/kid_tip: Watch for slippery snow. There are no sled rentals for children.
restaurants/0/name: Gyutan Sumiyaki Rikyu West Exit Main Branch
restaurants/0/signature: Gyutan set meal (with barley rice and oxtail soup)
restaurants/0/desc: The main branch of Sendai's most famous gyutan chain grills thickly sliced beef tongue over charcoal and serves it with barley rice and oxtail soup. The menu is varied, so kids can have a hamburger steak or curry.
restaurants/0/tips/0: Lunch wait of 30 minutes or more
restaurants/0/tips/1: There is also a branch on Gyutan Street, 3rd floor of Sendai Station
restaurants/1/desc: This is the original shop that started grilling gyutan in 1948, and you eat while watching it grilled over charcoal at the counter. The menu is just the one gyutan set meal, so ordering is simple and tables turn over fast.
restaurants/1/tips/1: Seating is limited, so avoid the lunch peak
restaurants/1/tips/2: The flavor is on the salty side
restaurants/2/name: Gyutan Kaku Brand Dome Main Branch
restaurants/2/signature: Gyutan set meal and gyutan tataki
restaurants/2/desc: Locals rate its thick, tender gyutan highly. Gyutan tataki (lightly seared beef tongue) and drink snacks are available, so it is good for a casual evening drink.
restaurants/2/tips/1: It is inside the arcade, so it is convenient even in the rain
restaurants/3/name: Gyutan Gisuke Ekimae Chuo Main Branch
restaurants/3/signature: Gyutan set meal (choice of salt, miso or soy sauce)
restaurants/3/desc: Founded in 1975, this gyutan specialist lets you choose from three seasonings (salt, miso or soy sauce), so families can share. It is close to the station, which makes it handy for your first meal after arriving or lunch before departure.
restaurants/3/tips/0: The wait tends to be shorter than at Rikyu
restaurants/3/tips/1: Also a branch on the 3rd floor of Sendai Station
restaurants/4/desc: This is Sendai's signature dessert shop, serving zunda (ground edamame) as a shake, located in Zunda Alley on the 3rd floor of the station. You can drink it as you walk, so it is a perfect snack on the go.
restaurants/4/tips/1: There is also an airport branch
restaurants/5/desc: Founded in 1877, this rice cake shop lets you eat zunda mochi made that day inside the shop. It uses little sugar, so the aroma of the edamame comes through, and locals recommend it as the best zunda.
restaurants/5/tips/0: Closes early if sold out for the day
restaurants/5/tips/2: We recommend the assortment of three kinds of mochi
restaurants/6/desc: This is a Sendai specialty sasa-kamaboko shop, and the hyotan-age sold in front of the shop is famous as a kids' snack. If you get a winning stick, you receive one more.
restaurants/6/tips/1: Kamaboko gift items can be packed with a cold pack
restaurants/7/signature: Zunda mochi, anmitsu and shaved ice
restaurants/7/desc: This Japanese dessert cafe with a garden sits in an arcade alley and serves zunda mochi and anmitsu with tea. It is a good place to rest while shopping, and the summer shaved ice is popular.
restaurants/7/tips/0: There are few seats, so we recommend 2:00 to 4:00 p.m.
restaurants/8/signature: Chuka soba (chicken broth soy sauce ramen)
restaurants/8/desc: This clear chicken broth soy sauce ramen is a regular favorite near the top of Sendai ramen rankings. It is not too strong, so it is easy to share with a child, and it is close to the station.
restaurants/8/hours: 11:00 to 15:00, 17:30 to 20:00 (closes when the soup runs out, to be confirmed)
restaurants/9/desc: Serinabe, a hot pot of Japanese parsley with the roots included, is a winter specialty of Sendai, and this izakaya helped make serinabe widely known. You can also enjoy Sanriku sashimi and local sake.
restaurants/9/tips/0: Serinabe is available only from November to March
restaurants/9/tips/2: Serinabe for one person is possible
restaurants/10/signature: Fried oyster set meal and raw oysters
restaurants/10/desc: This oyster specialist serves Miyagi oysters all year, and the fried oyster set meal is a popular lunch. In winter it offers raw oysters and oyster hot pot, and in summer iwagaki (rock oysters).
restaurants/10/tips/0: Oyster season is October to March
restaurants/10/tips/1: There is a fish set meal for those who can't eat oysters
restaurants/11/desc: This antique cafe with a riverside terrace behind Jozenji-dori is the place Sendai women recommend most. It is nice for resting with a slice of cake after your walk along the avenue.
restaurants/11/tips/0: Terrace seats are best in spring and autumn
restaurants/12/signature: Conger eel rice bowl and fried oyster set meal
restaurants/12/desc: This is the most popular seafood restaurant on the Matsushima shore, and its signature dish is the Matsushima conger eel (anago) rice bowl. From the 2nd-floor windows you can see Godaido and the sea.
restaurants/12/tips/0: Lunch waits are long, so go right when it opens at 11:00
restaurants/12/tips/1: Oyster set meal in oyster season
restaurants/13/cuisine: Grilled oysters and seafood rice bowls
restaurants/13/signature: All-you-can-eat grilled oysters (timed) and Zuiganji oyster rice bowl
restaurants/13/desc: The first floor has a seafood market and rice bowl shops, and the neighboring Yakigaki House is famous for its timed all-you-can-eat grilled oysters. It is a good place for each family member to choose what they want.
restaurants/13/hours: Market 8:00 to 17:00, Yakigaki House around 10:00 to 15:00 (to be confirmed)
restaurants/13/tips/0: All-you-can-eat oysters are around ¥2,500 for 45 minutes (estimate)
restaurants/13/tips/1: Oysters are biggest from October to March
restaurants/14/desc: The experience of grilling leaf-shaped sasa-kamaboko fish cakes yourself over charcoal and eating them is popular with kids. It sits between the cruise pier and Zuiganji, so it is a good snack stop.
restaurants/14/tips/0: The experience is around ¥300 per piece
restaurants/14/tips/1: Fish cakes can be packed as gifts
restaurants/15/desc: This is the best-known sushi shop in Shiogama, a tuna landing port, serving Sanriku fish with refinement. Stopping here for lunch on the way to Matsushima makes the itinerary flow naturally.
restaurants/15/tips/1: The lunch nigiri set is the best value
restaurants/15/tips/2: 10 minutes on foot from Hon-Shiogama Station
restaurants/16/desc: Right in front of Hon-Shiogama Station, this sushi shop serves an assortment of seasonal fish at relatively reasonable prices. It has a branch in Sendai too, so if you are short on time you can eat inside the station.
restaurants/17/desc: This restaurant at the entrance to the Yamadera hiking trail serves Yamagata-style ita soba and tamakonnyaku (soy sauce konjac skewers). It is nice to eat a hearty meal before the climb, or finish with cool soba after coming down.
restaurants/17/tips/0: Plan your meal around the Senzan Line timetable
restaurants/18/desc: This small supermarket in Akiu Onsen sells the legendary ohagi, said to sell 5,000 a day. The red bean paste is not too sweet and the pieces are large, so one is enough as a snack after the hot spring.
restaurants/18/tips/0: Often sold out in the afternoon
restaurants/19/desc: This soba shop sits on the path from Yamadera Station to the trailhead, and its signature dish is Yamagata-style ita soba served on a wooden board. It is a good alternative when Fumotoya is crowded, and the tamakonnyaku skewers in front of the shop are a popular snack.
restaurants/19/tips/0: Plan your meal around the Senzan Line timetable
restaurants/20/signature: Miyagi vegetable lunch plate and handmade desserts
restaurants/20/desc: This cafe restaurant in a renovated old farmhouse in Akiu Onsen village serves a lunch plate and desserts made with local vegetables and rice. It is right next to Raira Gorge, so it is a good place to rest after a walk.
restaurants/20/tips/0: Lunch is limited in quantity, so go early
restaurants/21/name: Mitsui Outlet Sendai Port Food Court
restaurants/21/cuisine: Food court (ramen, gyutan, udon and more)
restaurants/21/signature: Gyutan rice bowl and kids' set
restaurants/21/desc: This is the easiest lunch on a day combining the aquarium and the outlet, with ramen, gyutan, udon and other shops gathered together. Kids' chairs and a kids' menu make it convenient for family trips.
restaurants/21/tips/0: Seats are competitive at weekend lunch
restaurants/21/tips/1: Ask at the entrance whether you can re-enter the aquarium
hotels/0/desc: This JR-group hotel connects directly to the west exit of Sendai Station. Matsushima, Yamadera and the airport are all reached straight from the station, making it the most convenient base for day trips. The rooms are spacious and the breakfast buffet includes zunda and gyutan.
hotels/0/pts/0: Directly connected to the station, so no walking with luggage
hotels/0/pts/1: Within walking distance of Gyutan Street and the arcades
hotels/0/pts/2: The East Building has newer rooms
hotels/1/desc: This high-rise hotel occupies the 25th floor and above of the Sendai Trust Tower, and the room windows look out over the city to the Pacific. The bathrooms are large and the lounge breakfast is excellent, so it suits a celebration trip.
hotels/1/pts/1: 8 minutes on foot to the station and arcades
hotels/2/desc: Located between the arcades and Jozenji-dori, it has a convenient route for shopping and walks, and the top-floor public bath gives a night view of the city. The calm room design gets good reviews from women travelers.
hotels/2/pts/0: Top-floor public bath with a view
hotels/2/pts/1: 5 minutes on foot to the arcades and Jozenji-dori
hotels/3/desc: This business hotel chain has a natural hot spring public bath and a free late-night soba snack, and offers high satisfaction for the price. It sits between the station and the arcades, so you can walk anywhere.
hotels/3/pts/1: Free late-night snack and ice cream
hotels/3/pts/2: 7 minutes on foot to the station
hotels/4/desc: Run by a family that served as bath keepers to the Date clan, now in its 34th generation, this is Akiu's leading ryokan, with riverside open-air baths and kaiseki dinners as the highlights. A shuttle from Sendai Station makes getting there easy.

bplan/0/desc: On a rainy day, instead of strolling Jozenji-dori, look down on the avenue from inside the glass building and rest at the 1st-floor cafe and shop. Closed on the fourth Thursday (to be confirmed).
bplan/1/desc: When it rains or you miss the last Loople bus, see the Date clan relics and the armor experience instead of the castle ruins. Closed Mondays, so check the date.
bplan/2/desc: When a preschooler is tired or on a rainy afternoon, use this indoor facility within walking distance of the station instead of Matsushima or Yamadera.
bplan/3/desc: If the cruise is canceled or your child dislikes boats, swap in the aquarium and Ferris wheel, 20 minutes away on the Senseki Line.
bplan/4/desc: If you have an hour to spare in Matsushima, ride up by taxi in 5 minutes and look over the whole bay. A must in cherry blossom season.
bplan/5/desc: On the way to Matsushima, get off one stop early to add the stone-step shrine and tuna sushi.
bplan/6/desc: It is on the route to Yamadera by rental car or the Senzan Line. If you can't reserve a tour, a walk among the buildings in the forest is still nice.
bplan/7/desc: If you have a car and a spare day, combine it with Yamadera and continue to the gas-lamp hot spring town. A day trip by public transport is a 6-hour round trip, so we don't recommend it.
nearby_alternatives/0/reason: If your goals in the same Tohoku region are the Nebuta Festival, the cherry blossoms of Hirosaki Castle and apples, choose Aomori. It is 1.5 hours from Sendai by Shinkansen, so it is also easy to connect
nearby_alternatives/1/reason: For a trip centered on rice, sake and seafood, and when you want something quieter than Sendai. The winter snow scenery and hot springs are equally strong points
nearby_alternatives/2/reason: If a direct flight to Sendai is expensive or the schedule doesn't fit, you can add Sendai and Matsushima as a day trip or one night, 1.5 hours from Tokyo by Shinkansen
